description:
Team from Paraná, Brazil

Paraná is a major agricultural state, so we're building a tool that uses NASA satellite data (rainfall, soil moisture, climate) to help local farmers adapt to drought and climate change.
summary: In southern Brazil the same field gives two crops a year: soybeans in summer, then "safrinha" (second-crop) corn right after. The soybean planting date decides when the corn reaches its critical stage (flowering and grain fill), and so whether it meets frost or drought. weharvest is a web app, in English and Portuguese, that turns 45 years of NASA POWER daily data (1981-2026) into one plain answer: "If I plant soybeans on this date, in how many of the last 45 seasons would the corn have met frost or drought?" It works for any municipality in southern Brazil, adds NASA SRTM relief to spot cold-air lowlands, and compares three rotations (soybean-corn, soybean-wheat, soybean-corn+brachiaria) by frost, drought and bare-soil erosion, re-ordered by what the farmer values and cannot do. This addresses Field Shift by helping farmers adapt planting dates and rotations to a changing climate with NASA data, at the scale of their own field. We tested it against 113 weather stations, 269 municipalities' official yields and the real 2026 drought and frost in Paraná. It supports the farmer and the agronomist; it does not replace them.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

In southern Brazil the same field gives two crops a year: soybeans in summer, then "safrinha" (second-crop) corn right after. The soybean planting date decides when the corn reaches its critical stage (flowering and grain fill), and so whether it meets frost or drought. weharvest (https://weharvest.vercel.app) answers one question for the farmer's own municipality: "If I plant soybeans on this date, in how many of the last 45 seasons would the corn have met frost or drought in its critical stage?" The answer comes in plain words ("4 in every 10 years", Low/Medium/High), with the best date for frost and a chart comparing every planting date. It then compares three rotations (soybean → corn, soybean → wheat, soybean → corn + brachiaria grass) by frost, drought and erosion. The farmer says what matters most (income, protecting soil and water, or balance) and what they cannot do (no wheat buyer or machinery, cannot manage brachiaria, little water); the app re-orders the options and says why, without changing the risk numbers. Extra sections show a 16-day "can I plant this week?" check, how many days a year the soil is left bare and how much rain falls on it, an optional El Niño / La Niña recount, and a "2026 proof" that sets the NASA data next to the real April drought and May frost reported by Paraná's agriculture department (Deral).

HOW IT WORKS

NASA data is the core of every answer. For any municipality in southern Brazil (search by name or use the device's location), the browser downloads 45 years of NASA POWER daily data (1981–2026: minimum air temperature, rainfall and root-zone soil wetness) straight from NASA in about 2 seconds, and a small risk engine runs on the device. For each past season it builds the soybean-to-corn calendar and checks the corn's critical stage for frost (2 m minimum temperature ≤ 3 °C; +1 °C in lowlands) and drought (15+ dry days, or soil wetness among the driest 20% for those dates). NASA SRTM elevation shows the relief around each point, and a GPS check tells whether a plot sits in a lowland where cold air pools. NOAA's RONI index classifies each season as El Niño, La Niña or neutral. Three demonstration municipalities are stored with the code so the app also works offline for them.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Farmers and agronomists already ask this question every spring, but the answer usually comes from memory of the last bad year. weharvest turns 45 years of satellite-based records into a number anyone can read, in English or Portuguese, and shows how many years each number rests on. The aim is to help farmers choose planting dates and rotations that lose less to frost and drought and leave the soil covered longer, as the climate shifts. It supports the decision; it does not replace the farmer or the agronomist.

TESTED AGAINST THE REAL WORLD

We wrote each test's rules before running it. Against 113 weather stations in southern Brazil (307,517 days), NASA POWER's minimum temperature tracks the measured one (correlation 0.90), and the app's frost seasons agreed with the stations in 84% of cases. Against official IBGE yields in 269 municipalities (5,652 municipality-years), years the app flagged for drought produced about 7.5% less second-crop corn. Weather stations in lowlands were measurably colder, confirming that terrain position matters for frost.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19 and Tailwind CSS 4; risk engine written as pure functions with 61 automated tests (Node's built-in test runner); Node scripts for data download and validation; hosted on Vercel, source on GitHub. Data: NASA POWER Daily API, NASA SRTM 30 m (via OpenTopoData), NOAA CPC RONI, Open-Meteo (forecast and place search), IBGE municipal crop survey, INMET station data and Deral reports. No hardware was needed: it runs in any web browser, on a computer or a phone.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Instead of a map of climate layers, it starts from the decision the farmer actually makes (the soybean date) and follows its effect into the next crop, months later. It ranks rotations by the farmer's own priorities and limits rather than by a hidden score. And it is transparent: every threshold is shown as a hypothesis, and the validation results are on screen.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

The app works on computers and phones; for use in the field, often outdoors and with weak signal, we chose plain language, large type, few taps and offline demo data. NASA POWER is a ~50 km grid and measures air at 2 m, not at the plant, so we set the frost limit at 3 °C based on Embrapa studies and added the lowland check. Crop cycles and thresholds vary with cultivar and region, so they are labeled as hypotheses to validate with agronomists and Brazil's official ZARC zoning. The app only computes south of 22°S, where its rules were calibrated, and it only sends the typed place name or coordinates; nothing personal is stored.
